commands.name: dataviz
commands.description: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. commands.name: artifact-capabilities

commands.name: update-config
commands.description: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. content.content: Topic: why the number of subsets of an n-element set doubles each time n grows by one

input.message:
Why the number of subsets doubles when n grows by one

Start with the smallest case. A set with no elements, the empty set, has exactly one subset: itself. A set with one element, say {a}, has two: the empty set and {a}. A set with two elements, {a, b}, has four: the empty set, {a}, {b}, and {a, b}. Each time an element is added, the count goes from 1 to 2 to 4, and the pattern suggests that a set with n elements has 2^n subsets. The reason this holds, and why the rule is doubling rather than some other growth, comes from looking at what a single new element does to the subsets that already exist.

Take any set of n elements and let S be the collection of all its subsets. Now add one new element, call it x, to form a set with n + 1 elements. Every subset of the new set falls into exactly one of two groups. Either it contains x or it does not. If a subset does not contain x, it is already a subset of the original set, so it is one of the members of S. If it does contain x, then removing x leaves a subset of the original set. So the subsets of the new set split cleanly into two families, and each family is in one-to-one correspondence with S.

The correspondence is simple. Pair each old subset T with two new subsets: T itself (without x) and T together with x. Every old subset gives exactly two new subsets, and every new subset arises from exactly one old subset, namely the one obtained by deleting x. No subset is counted twice and none is missed. Therefore the number of subsets of the new set is twice the number of subsets of the old set. If the old set had 2^n subsets, the new one has 2 times 2^n, which is 2^(n+1).

A useful way to see the same fact is through choices. To build a subset of a given set, go through its elements one at a time and decide, for each, whether to include it. Each decision is independent of the others and has exactly two options: in or out. By the multiplication principle, when there are n independent two-way choices, the total number of outcomes is 2 multiplied by itself n times, which is 2^n. Adding an element adds one more independent two-way choice, and an extra factor of 2 is exactly what the multiplication principle predicts.

Binary strings give another picture of the same idea. Label the elements 1 through n, and represent a subset by a string of n bits, where a 1 in position i means element i is included and a 0 means it is excluded. There are exactly 2^n strings of length n, since each position can be 0 or 1 independently. The subsets and the strings are in perfect correspondence, and lengthening the string by one position doubles the number of possibilities.

The result can also be checked by a count sorted by size. The number of subsets of size k in an n-element set is the binomial coefficient C(n, k). Summing over all k from 0 to n gives the total, and the binomial theorem says that this sum equals (1 + 1)^n, which is 2^n. The two arguments agree, which is reassuring, because the doubling argument does not depend on any particular size.

Two points are worth keeping in mind. First, the empty set and the full set are both counted, which is why the base case is 1 and not 0. Second, the doubling is not a coincidence of small numbers. Each new element creates a fresh, independent yes-or-no decision that applies to every subset already counted, so the total must double. This is why the number of subsets grows exponentially: the growth is multiplicative in the number of elements, not additive. A set of 10 elements has 1,024 subsets, and a set of 20 has over a million, all from the same simple rule that each element doubles the count.

Every subset of the new set falls into exactly one of two groups. Either it contains x or it does not. If a subset does not contain x, it is already a subset of the original set, so it is one of the members of S. If it does contain x, then removing x leaves a subset of the original set. So the subsets of the new set split cleanly into two families, and each family is in one-to-one correspondence with S.

The correspondence is simple. Pair each old subset T with two new subsets: T itself (without x) and T together with x. Each new element creates a fresh, independent yes-or-no decision that applies to every subset already counted, so the total must double.
